displayQuote: Reason is the Devil's greatest whore

meta.title: Who really said "Reason is the Devil's greatest whore"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: Genuine Luther: his last Wittenberg sermon, 17 January 1546 (WA 51:126). But the long viral 'noxious whore… throw dung' paragraph is a stitched composite.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'Reason is the Devil's greatest whore'?
meta.ogDescription: Genuine Luther, from his last Wittenberg sermon (17 Jan 1546). The longer viral paragraph is stitched together from several places; one translation says 'foremost whore'.

answer.label: Spoken by
answer.sourceLine: From Luther’s last sermon in Wittenberg, preached on Romans 12:3 on 17 January 1546 and written down by people who heard it. The German reads “Vernunft … ist die höchste Hur, die der Teufel hat” (WA 51:126). This exact English wording is printed in Jacques Maritain’s Three Reformers (London, 1928).

source.heading: The source

docMeta.dd: German, written down by hearers · WA 51:126 · Erlangen ed. 16:142ff
Jacques Maritain, Three Reformers (London: Sheed & Ward, 1928), p. 32

source.excerpt: Reason is the devil’s greatest whore; by nature and manner of being she is a noxious whore; she is a prostitute, the devil’s appointed whore; a whore eaten by scab and leprosy who ought to be trodden under foot and destroyed, she and her wisdom… Throw dung in her face to make her ugly. She is, and she ought to be, drowned in baptism…
trail: Wikiquote’s sourced quotes for Luther list “[reason] is the Devil’s greatest whore” and give the German as “Vernunft … ist die höchste Hur, die der Teufel hat.” They cite Martin Luther’s Last Sermon in Wittenberg … 17 January 1546, Weimar edition 51:126. Wikiquote ↗

The standard English edition, Luther’s Works 51:373–374, says: “But the devil’s bride, reason, the lovely whore comes in and wants to be wise … for she is the foremost whore the devil has.” This is the passage as James Swan quotes it. Beggars All ↗

Jacques Maritain’s Three Reformers (London: Sheed & Ward, “first published September, 1928”) has the exact wording on p. 32, introduced as from “the last sermon preached at Wittenberg.” Its footnote reads “Erl., 16, 142 to 148 (1546). Cf. Denifle-Paquier, III, 277-278.” Internet Archive ↗
Swan traces the internet’s version back to p. 26 of Peter F. Wiener’s Martin Luther: Hitler’s Spiritual Ancestor, which copies Maritain word for word. Beggars All ↗
source.excerptNote: Maritain footnotes this whole paragraph to “Erl., 16, 142 to 148 (1546).” His ellipses mark jumps across those pages, so the paragraph is a composite of separate sentences. The first sentence is the famous line. Fortress Press’s Luther’s Works vol. 51 translates the same sentence “for she is the foremost whore the devil has” (as quoted on Beggars All ↗).

sourceLink.text: Maritain, Three Reformers (1928), full text at the Internet Archive

source.rightsNote: Luther’s 1546 German sermon has long been in the public domain. The English wording shown here is from Maritain’s Three Reformers, first published in London in September 1928. Anything published before 1931 is public domain in the US. Other translations are a separate matter: Luther’s Works vol. 51 (Fortress Press, 1959), for example, is still in copyright.

author.name: Martin Luther
author.heading: About Martin Luther
author.bio: Martin Luther was an Augustinian friar and Wittenberg professor whose attack on indulgences began the Protestant Reformation. He preached constantly. Many of his sermons survive only because hearers, chiefly his secretary Georg Rörer, wrote them down, and this one is among them. Luther praised reason as a gift for running earthly life, but he attacked it hard whenever it set itself above faith.

misattribution.heading: Real line, embellished quote
misattribution.intro: Luther really said this. What goes wrong is everything people attach to it: a stitched-together paragraph, and claims that one sentence shows his whole view of reason.

items.scope: The long “noxious whore … throw dung in her face … to the closets” paragraph
items.why: Maritain footnotes the whole paragraph to six pages of the Erlangen edition (16:142–148), and his ellipses mark the jumps. James Swan shows how the paragraph travelled from Denifle to Maritain, then to Wiener, then online, losing its context along the way. Beggars All ↗
The German is “die höchste Hur, die der Teufel hat” (Wikiquote ↗). Maritain’s English says “greatest”. Luther’s Works 51 says “the foremost whore the devil has”. Both translate the same sentence.

The Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy says Luther’s relationship to philosophy “should not be judged only by his famous statement that ‘reason is the devil’s whore,’” and that he gave reason important roles in life and in the community. IEP ↗

misattribution.truthLine: Luther did say it, in his last Wittenberg sermon of 17 January 1546 (WA 51:126). The long paragraph usually quoted after it is a translated composite. Wikiquote ↗

context.heading: What Luther meant
lead: The sermon is on Romans 12:3, Paul’s warning not to think of oneself more highly than one ought. Luther contrasts sins anyone can see, such as usury, gluttony and adultery, with reason. Reason is subtler: it “wants to be wise” and mistakes its own ideas for the Holy Spirit. As Swan quotes the sermon, Luther’s remedy is that “Reason must be subject and obedient to this faith” (Luther’s Works 51:379). Beggars All ↗

So the target is reason that sets itself up as judge in spiritual matters, not thinking in general. The Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy says Luther believed reason was “necessary for a good and just society.” In its reading, reason is “the devil’s whore” for him only because, in theology, “it asks the wrong questions and looks in the wrong direction for answers.” IEP ↗

sourcesVerified.claim: Wikiquote's sourced quotes list '[reason] is the Devil's greatest whore', give the German 'Vernunft … ist die höchste Hur, die der Teufel hat', and cite the Last Sermon in Wittenberg, 17 January 1546, WA 51:126

Maritain, Three Reformers (London: Sheed & Ward, first published September 1928), p. 32, prints 'Reason is the devil's greatest whore…' as from the last sermon preached at Wittenberg, with footnote 36 'Erl., 16, 142 to 148 (1546). Cf. Denifle-Paquier, III, 277-278'

LW 51:373–374 renders the passage 'the devil's bride, reason, the lovely whore … for she is the foremost whore the devil has'; LW 51:379 'Reason must be subject and obedient to this faith'; the viral paragraph is copied from Wiener p. 26, who copied Maritain; the sermon was recorded by Rörer and Tucher, 17 January 1546

IEP: Luther's relationship to philosophy 'should not be judged only by his famous statement that reason is the devil's whore'; reason is 'necessary for a good and just society'; it is the devil's whore because 'it asks the wrong questions and looks in the wrong direction for answers'
Luther's Works vol. 51, Sermons I, edited by John W. Doberstein, Fortress Press, publication date 1959, includes 'The Last Sermon in Wittenberg, 1546'
